stops.teaser: A government building copied from a Roman temple in France, designed by Thomas Jefferson.
stops.map: Virginia State Capitol, 1000 Bank St, Richmond, VA
stops.clue: Go to Capitol Square in downtown Richmond. Look for the white building with a row of tall columns and a triangle-shaped roof over the front, like a temple.
stops.safety: Capitol Square is a working government site. Stay on the paths, use crosswalks, and check visiting hours and security rules before going inside.

story: The Virginia State Capitol houses the General Assembly, which traces back to the House of Burgesses first meeting in 1619. Wikipedia calls it the oldest elected legislative body in North America.

Thomas Jefferson is credited with the overall design, together with French architect Charles-Louis Clérisseau. It is modeled after the Maison Carrée, an ancient Roman temple in Nîmes. Construction began in 1785 and was completed in 1788. This is the eighth building to serve as Virginia's statehouse, mostly because of fires.

From 1861 to 1865 the building was the capitol of the Confederate States of America. In the early 20th century two wings were added, which gave the building its present appearance. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1960.
stops.fact: It is the eighth Virginia statehouse.
stops.disputed: Many people think the Capitol has always had wings on each side. Wikipedia says the two wings were added in the early 20th century.

claims.t: Construction on the Capitol began in 1785.
claims.why: Wikipedia: construction began in 1785 and was completed in 1788.

claims.t: The Capitol was designed by a team of Roman architects.
claims.why: Jefferson and French architect Clérisseau designed it, modeled on a Roman temple.

story: St. John's is the oldest church in the city of Richmond. It was built in 1741 by Colonel Richard Randolph, and the Church Hill neighborhood was named for it. It stands at 2401 East Broad Street and is a National Historic Landmark.

The church was the site of two important conventions in the years before the American Revolution. It is famous as the place where Founding Father Patrick Henry gave his speech at the Second Virginia Convention.
The parish grew out of earlier ones. The first, Henrico Parish Church, was at Henricus in 1611. Henricus was destroyed in 1622 and was never rebuilt.
stops.fact: The hill is named for the church.
stops.disputed: Many people assume the church was built in the 1770s, when the speech was given. Wikipedia says it was built in 1741.

claims.why: Wikipedia: built in 1741 by Colonel Richard Randolph.

claims.why: Wikipedia says the Church Hill district was named for the church.

stops.name: Jefferson Hotel
stops.teaser: A grand hotel that once had alligators swimming in the lobby.
stops.map: The Jefferson Hotel, 101 W Franklin St, Richmond, VA
stops.clue: Go to Franklin Street at Adams Street, in downtown Richmond. Look for the big hotel with a tall clock tower and a rich, cream-colored front.
stops.safety: Franklin Street has traffic. Use crosswalks, and be polite in the lobby, since it is a working hotel.

story: Tobacco baron Lewis Ginter planned the hotel as a top property for the city. Carrère and Hastings, the New York architects who later designed the New York Public Library, designed it in the Spanish Baroque style. It opened on October 31, 1895.

On March 29, 1901, a fire destroyed three-fifths of the hotel. The marble statue of Thomas Jefferson was carried to safety, but its head broke off in the rescue. It was repaired later. The hotel reopened in 1907.

The actor David Niven wrote that he saw a full-sized alligator swimming in a pool near the reception desk. Old Pompey, the last alligator in the Palm Court pools, lived until 1948. Today bronze alligators decorate the hotel.
stops.fact: The last alligator was named Old Pompey.
stops.disputed: Many people think the alligators are still there. Wikipedia says the last one lived until 1948, and now there are bronze statues of them.

claims.t: The hotel's lobby still has live alligators.
claims.why: Old Pompey, the last one, lived until 1948.

stops.name: Main Street Station
stops.teaser: A train station with a clock tower that was flooded, burned and brought back.
stops.map: Main Street Station, 1500 E Main St, Richmond, VA
stops.clue: Go to East Main Street at 15th Street, in the Shockoe Bottom neighborhood. Look for the red-brick station with a clock tower and a steep red-tile roof.
stops.safety: Trains and highway traffic are close by. Stay off the tracks and platforms unless you are boarding, and use crosswalks.

story: Main Street Station was built in 1901 by two railroads, the Seaboard Air Line and the Chesapeake and Ohio, which had each used separate stations before. The Philadelphia firm of Wilson, Harris, and Richards designed it in the Second Renaissance Revival style. The people of Richmond call it The Clock Tower.

It became a National Historic Landmark in 1976. In 1972, Hurricane Agnes flooded the station so badly that Amtrak moved most of its Richmond stops to a smaller station in the suburbs in 1975. Fires hit the building in 1976 and 1983.
After the 1983 fire it was renovated and reopened as a shopping mall in 1985, but the mall closed in 1986. Amtrak serves the station today, and it is also a stop on the GRTC Pulse bus line.
stops.fact: Locals call it The Clock Tower.
stops.disputed: Many people think a station this old must always have been used for trains. Wikipedia says it was a shopping mall for a short time in the 1980s.

claims.t: Main Street Station was built in 1901.
The station was a mall for more than thirty years.
claims.why: The mall opened in 1985 and closed in 1986.
